title: RSA step by step
syllabusUnit: Unit III: RSA Algorithm & Trapdoor One-Way Functions
covers: Key generation, encrypt/decrypt, why factoring is hard
learningGoals: You will be able to calculate RSA keys from tiny primes p and q.
You will be able to encrypt plaintext C = M^e mod n and decrypt M = C^d mod n.
You will be able to explain why OAEP padding is required to prevent textbook RSA attacks.

lessonCards.title: RSA Key Generation
lessonCards.analogy: Two secret keys: one public padlock that anyone can snap shut, and one private key that only you hold to open it.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Pick primes p, q. Compute n = p * q and phi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1). Pick e coprime to phi(n). Find d = e⁻¹ mod phi(n). Public key is (e, n); private key is d.

lessonCards.title: Encrypting & Decrypting
lessonCards.analogy: Closing the public padlock with math power e; opening it with secret key power d.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Encryption: Ciphertext C = M^e mod n. Decryption: Message M = C^d mod n. Euler's theorem guarantees (M^e)^d = M^(e*d) = M^1 = M mod n.
lessonCards.example: Encrypting M = 7: C = 7^3 mod 33 = 343 mod 33 = 13. Decrypting: 13^7 mod 33 = 7.

lessonCards.title: The Textbook RSA Trap: OAEP Padding
lessonCards.analogy: Never send a naked secret: wrap it in random bubble-wrap before locking it in the box.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Textbook RSA is deterministic: encrypting 'YES' always produces the same ciphertext. Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (OAEP) adds random noise before encrypting.
lessonCards.example: PKCS#1 v2.1 OAEP padding prevents chosen-ciphertext and Bleichenbacher attacks.

questions.prompt: In RSA with p = 5 and q = 11, what is the modulus n and totient phi(n)?
wrongExplanations: Correct! n = 55, phi(n) = 40.
54 would assume n is prime.
5 * 11 does not equal 50.
16 is the sum.
questions.realWorldExample: Rivest, Shamir, and Adleman published RSA in 1977 at MIT.

questions.prompt: Given public exponent e = 3 and phi(n) = 40, what is the private decryption exponent d (such that (e * d) mod phi(n) = 1)?
questions.realWorldExample: Extended Euclidean algorithm calculates d from e and phi(n) in logarithmic steps.

questions.prompt: Why is 'Textbook RSA' (encrypting raw message M without padding) completely insecure in production systems?
options: It is deterministic (same message yields same ciphertext) and vulnerable to chosen-ciphertext attacks
Computers refuse to compile textbook formulas
questions.explanation: Without randomized padding, attackers can guess small messages or multiply ciphertexts together due to RSA's multiplicative homomorphic property.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Unpadded RSA leaks equality of plaintexts and allows Bleichenbacher oracle attacks.
Keys do not expire automatically.
65537 (2^16 + 1) is prime and odd.
Compilers execute the arithmetic without awareness of context.
questions.realWorldExample: OAEP padding (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) is mandated by RFC 8017.

questions.prompt: What is the most common public exponent e chosen in modern production RSA implementations?
questions.explanation: e = 65537 has only two '1' bits in binary (10000000000000001), allowing fast encryption in only 17 operations while resisting small-exponent attacks.
wrongExplanations: Correct! 65537 is the global industry standard public exponent.
e = 3 was historical but vulnerable to broadcast Coppersmith attacks when padding is weak.
e cannot be even because it must be coprime to phi(n).
Arbitrary round numbers offer no binary speed advantages.
questions.realWorldExample: Fermat prime F4 = 65537 balances high speed with strong security.

questions.prompt: If an attacker can factor the public modulus n into primes p and q, what secret can they immediately calculate?
options: They can calculate phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) and derive the private key d
They can read the server's hard drive directly
They can change the server's IP address
questions.explanation: Knowing p and q reveals phi(n), allowing the attacker to compute modular inverse d = e^-1 mod phi(n), totally compromising the private key.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Factoring n instantly destroys RSA private key secrecy.
Factoring does not give remote disk access.
Network routing is unaffected.
Internet operations continue.
questions.realWorldExample: This is why RSA keys must be at least 2048 bits (and recommended 3072 bits today).

questions.prompt: How are public and private keys shared in RSA?
options: The public key (e, n) is shared with everyone; the private key d is kept strictly secret
Both keys are posted publicly on Twitter
Both keys are kept secret and never shared
The private key is sent in clear HTTP
questions.explanation: Public key cryptography allows anyone to encrypt using (e, n), while only the owner can decrypt using private key d.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Public keys are openly distributed; private keys must never leave secure storage.
Publishing the private key allows anyone to decrypt your data.
If both are secret, nobody can send you encrypted data.
Sending private keys over clear HTTP causes immediate compromise.
questions.realWorldExample: SSL/TLS certificates openly publish RSA public keys to every connecting browser.

ashRecap: RSA locks data with public numbers (e, n) and unlocks it with private key d. Padding with OAEP keeps it bulletproof against eavesdroppers!
